articles.title: Beyond microchips, Trump takes aim at China's growing AI footprint in US
articles.summary: The Trump administration is considering a new move to curb China's growing influence in the American artificial intelligence industry, weighing a proposal
articles.body: The Trump administration is considering a new move to curb China's growing influence in the American artificial intelligence industry, weighing a proposal that would require US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models.According to a Reuters report, the proposal has been discussed by the US treasury department and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), with three people familiar with the matter saying it could require companies to disclose their use of Chinese AI models on their websites.The proposal could affect companies such as Airbnb, which uses Alibaba's Qwen AI model to power its customer service agent. However, it remains unclear whether the administration will take the proposal forward or introduce it through a formal rulemaking process.Under the proposal, companies using Chinese AI models would have to publicly identify their use of the technology on their websites. The move would not immediately restrict or prohibit their use of these models but would make their reliance on Chinese AI visible to customers, investors and policymakers.Airbnb, one of the companies cited in the report, said its AI operations run overwhelmingly on US-origin models. It added that its limited use of China-origin models takes place through approved US-based service providers, with data and operations kept separate and protected.The proposal comes amid growing concerns in Washington over the rapid adoption of Chinese AI models by American businesses.Models such as Alibaba's Qwen, DeepSeek and Moonshot AI's Kimi are gaining ground because they are cheaper than proprietary alternatives from US companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, while offering competitive performance.US officials fear that wider adoption could make American companies increasingly dependent on Chinese-developed AI technology, creating potential security vulnerabilities and giving Beijing greater influence over the technology powering US businesses.The concern is particularly pronounced around open-weight AI models, whose core components are publicly available and can be downloaded, modified and deployed by companies on their own infrastructure. US lawmakers fear that their growing adoption could create long-term dependence on Chinese technology, even when the models are operated within the United States.The administration is now exploring a disclosure-based approach to address these concerns, rather than imposing an outright ban on Chinese AI models or introducing fresh restrictions on American businesses.The proposed disclosure requirement could also serve as a 'name and shame' campaign, putting companies using Chinese AI under public scrutiny. By making such usage visible, the administration could expose businesses to questions from investors, customers and policymakers over their reliance on Chinese technology, potentially encouraging them to shift towards American alternatives.Republican Representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, welcomed the proposal, saying disclosure was an important step in managing the potential risks posed by the spread of Chinese open-weight models in the US.The discussions come amid renewed pressure on the Trump administration to take a tougher stance on Chinese technology, following revelations involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy.The controversy has also brought fresh attention to cases of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled into China, raising questions over the enforcement of US export restrictions.The developments have intensified scrutiny of how American AI technology could reach China despite Washington's efforts to restrict its access to advanced semiconductors.While export controls target the hardware needed to develop powerful AI systems, the proposed disclosure requirement signals a growing concern over the spread of Chinese AI software within American businesses.You use AI every day. articles.title: A war bill for Russia? Europe's €45 billion Ukraine plan echoes Germany's WWI reparations
articles.summary: In 1921, Germany was ordered to pay 132 billion gold marks (around $33 billion at the time) in reparations for the destruction caused by World War I.
articles.body: In 1921, Germany was ordered to pay 132 billion gold marks (around $33 billion at the time) in reparations for the destruction caused by World War I. More than a century later, Europe is looking to make Russia pay for the devastation of another war on the continent.The European Union has proposed a €45 billion loan to Ukraine, with an unusual condition: Kyiv would repay the money only after Moscow compensates it for the destruction caused by its invasion.The proposal was announced by European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday as the bloc seeks to ensure that Ukraine can sustain its defence against Russia while keeping its economy running.She said Europe remained committed to supporting Kyiv despite the prolonged conflict, stressing that the bloc's backing would continue both during the war and after a peace settlement."Five years since the start of this war of aggression, Europe stands united. We are as committed as ever to support Ukraine in war and in peace," von der Leyen said.She also reiterated Europe's resolve to maintain pressure on Moscow while ensuring that Ukraine receives the financial assistance it needs.Under the proposed arrangement, the €45 billion loan would be divided into two parts, with up to €25 billion earmarked for military assistance and €20 billion for general budget support.The military funding would help Ukraine sustain its defence against Russian forces, while the remaining amount would support the country's government finances and essential expenditure.To finance the package, the European Commission plans to borrow on behalf of the 27-member bloc from international markets. The proposed loan would come on top of the €90 billion in assistance agreed by EU leaders for 2026 and 2027.The proposed arrangement draws an unusual link between Ukraine's financial recovery and Russia's responsibility for wartime destruction.Under the plan, Kyiv would not be required to repay the principal until it receives reparations, indemnities or another financial settlement from Moscow. The EU has also retained the option of using immobilised Russian cash balances in accordance with EU and international law to recover the money.The proposal would additionally allow revenues generated by frozen Russian sovereign assets to support repayment of eligible loans. However, the plan is yet to receive approval from EU member states and the European Parliament.The proposal brings back memories of the reparations imposed on Germany after World War I under the Treaty of Versailles in 1919.Under Article 231, Germany accepted responsibility for war-related damage suffered by the Allied powers, providing the basis for reparations claims. In 1921, the Allied Reparations Commission fixed Germany's bill at 132 billion gold marks (around $33 billion at the time).The burden became a major source of economic and political turmoil in the country. Germany's failure to meet payments led France and Belgium to occupy the Ruhr industrial region in 1923, while the reparations crisis contributed to the country's economic instability and hyperinflation.The reparations dispute continued to shape Germany's economic and political landscape for years. The Dawes Plan of 1924 restructured payments and brought in international financial assistance to stabilise the country's economy.The historical parallel is striking, but the circumstances are very different. Unlike Germany in 1921, Russia has not been defeated or agreed to a reparations settlement. Yet, through its proposed loan mechanism, Europe is attempting to ensure that the financial burden of rebuilding Ukraine does not fall on Kyiv alone.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: US will not have a Christian majority by 2027, religiously unaffiliated to make up 41%: Pew study
articles.summary: The United States is projected to lose its Christian majority by 2070, with the number of Christians expected to fall from about 217 million in 2020 to
articles.body: The United States is projected to lose its Christian majority by 2070, with the number of Christians expected to fall from about 217 million in 2020 to about 174 million by 2070, according to a new Pew Research Center study released on Wednesday.People who do not identify with any religion are projected to account for about 41 per cent of the US population by 2070. Christians, who currently form the country's largest religious group, are expected to make up less than half of the population if recent demographic trends continue.The study also projects that Jews, who were the third-largest religious group in the US in 2020, will be outnumbered by both Muslims and Hindus by 2070.Religious switching driving US shiftPew said the projected decline in the Christian population and rise in the religiously unaffiliated will largely be driven by people changing their religious identities. In the US, Christians tend to lose more followers through religious switching than they gain.The study also pointed to age differences between the groups. Americans who do not identify with any religion are younger, on average, than Christians. A younger population generally has greater potential to grow because more of its members are in their childbearing years.The trend is also expected to reshape Canada's religious composition. Christians are projected to fall below 50% of the Canadian population by 2030, while people with no religious affiliation are expected to outnumber Christians there by 2070.Muslims projected to overtake Christians globally by 2035Beyond North America, Pew's study projects a major shift in the global religious landscape, with Muslims expected to surpass Christians as the world's largest religious group by 2035.The report estimates that the world had 2.27 billion Christians and 2.02 billion Muslims in 2020. By 2035, the Muslim population is projected to reach 2.57 billion, compared with 2.52 billion Christians.If current trends continue, the number of Muslims worldwide could exceed 3.6 billion by 2070, while the Christian population is projected to remain just below 3 billion.Pew attributed much of the difference in growth rates to fertility. Muslim women had an average of 3.1 children during 2020-2025, compared with 2.5 among Christian women and 1.6 among women from other major religious groups.Pew senior demographer Conrad Hackett summed up the role of births in the shift by saying: “It's the babies.” He said conversion and other forms of religious switching play a much smaller role than fertility rates in explaining the growth.Africa to drive growth of Christianity and IslamThe study said much of the world's population growth over the coming decades is expected to take place in sub-Saharan Africa, where most people identify as either Christian or Muslim. Higher fertility and rising life expectancy in the region are expected to increase the numbers of both religious groups.By 2070, more than a quarter of the world's population is projected to live in sub-Saharan Africa. More than half of all Christians worldwide are also expected to live in the region.The Democratic Republic of the Congo is projected to overtake the US as the country with the largest Christian population.Meanwhile, Muslims are expected to account for 36% of the global population in 2070, up from 26% in 2020. Christians are projected to make up about 29%, broadly similar to their share in 2020.Hindus are expected to increase in absolute numbers, with India recording the largest growth, although their share of the global population is projected to decline. Buddhists, meanwhile, are expected to decrease both in number and as a share of the world's population.Pew's projections cover 201 countries and territories, accounting for 99.98% of the world's population. The estimates factor in fertility, mortality, migration, age profiles and religious switching, and assume that recently observed demographic trends continue.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP MP Anurag Thakur on Wednesday accused Congress leader Rahul Gandhi of attempting to tarnish India's image abroad, claiming that his remarks on the country's economy at Columbia University were aimed at grabbing headlines.Thakur described Rahul's alleged obsession with publicity as "headline phobia" and accused him of relying on foreign allies, funding and "toolkits" in his pursuit of power."Once again, Rahul Gandhi has attempted to tarnish India's image on foreign soil. He claimed these efforts would not succeed and that Gandhi's alleged supporters would eventually abandon him.Thakur's remarks came after Rahul, during a fireside chat at Columbia University in New York on Tuesday, described India as sitting on an "economic disaster". articles.title: In 1911, the Denver Mint made a $10 gold coin that spent decades in a paper envelope inside a family's safe-deposit box; heirs uncovered its rarity in 2026, and experts now expect it to fetch more than $500,000
articles.summary: A $10 gold coin struck at the Denver Mint in 1911 spent decades in a paper envelope inside a family safe deposit box, apparently unnoticed among a group
articles.body: A $10 gold coin struck at the Denver Mint in 1911 spent decades in a paper envelope inside a family safe deposit box, apparently unnoticed among a group of ordinary inherited coins. In 2026, the heirs had it graded and discovered that it was a rare 1911-D Indian Gold Eagle, one of the finest known examples of the date, according to GreatCollections and CoinWeek.The coin, graded PCGS MS 65 and approved by Certified Acceptance Corporation with a green sticker, is now being offered without reserve in a GreatCollections auction closing January 10, 2027. GreatCollections expects it to bring more than $500,000, and bidding had already reached $107,500 after 19 bids as of November 17.A coin hiding in plain sightThe family inherited roughly three dozen common, low grade pre 1933 American gold coins from a relative who worked for the CIA during the 1950s. Among them was the 1911-D $10 Indian Gold Eagle, which remained uncertified in an old paper envelope until earlier this year.GreatCollections president Ian Russell said the coin had been kept in the safe deposit box for years without anyone recognising its importance. He noted that the family had not said who the former CIA employee was or when the coin was purchased, and that nothing tied the coin itself to intelligence work.When PCGS examined the coin in 2026, it awarded an MS 65 grade, and CAC approved it with its coveted green sticker. GreatCollections describes the result as the second finest CAC endorsed example of the date.Why the coin is rareThe 1911-D Indian Gold Eagle is the lowest mintage regular issue in the Indian Head eagle series, with only 30,100 coins struck at the Denver Mint. PCGS estimates that about 1,650 examples survive across all grades, including roughly 275 in Mint State.Only five examples are believed to grade MS 65 or finer, according to PCGS estimates cited by CoinWeek. That scarcity helps explain why the newly discovered coin has drawn attention from collectors and auction watchers.The coin was designed by Augustus Saint Gaudens and weighs 16.718 grams, with a composition of 90 percent gold and 10 percent copper. Its Denver mintmark appears on the reverse near the left side of the arrow bundle.How the value was determinedThe newly discovered example carries a PCGS Price Guide valuation of $425,000, but GreatCollections expects it to sell for more. The auction house says the final price will depend on competitive bidding.The last PCGS MS 65 example of this date to sell at public auction brought $195,500 in 2007, according to PCGS CoinFacts. A separate 1911-D Indian Gold Eagle graded PCGS MS 66 with CAC and CMQ sold for $1.8 million in February 2026, setting a record for any circulation strike Indian Head $10.Those results help frame expectations for the current coin. While it is not the same grade as the $1.8 million example, its MS 65 status and CAC approval place it among the most desirable survivors of the date.What makes this discovery notableThe story stands out because the coin was not part of a high profile collection or a museum archive. It was sitting in a paper envelope inside a family safe deposit box, alongside coins that were considered common and low grade.That context makes the discovery more relatable. It shows how a valuable item can remain hidden in plain sight until someone decides to have it examined by a professional grading service.The case also highlights the importance of certification. Before grading, the coin looked like an ordinary inherited gold piece. After PCGS and CAC assessed it, it became one of the most important gold coins on the auction calendar.What happens nextThe coin is being offered without reserve, meaning there is no minimum price that must be met for it to sell. Bidding is scheduled to close on Sunday, January 10, 2027, at 6:30 p.m. Pacific Time.As of November 17, bidding had reached $107,500 after 19 bids. The final result will show whether the market agrees with GreatCollections’ expectation that the coin will bring more than $500,000.For the family, the discovery is a reminder that inherited items can carry unexpected value. For collectors, it is a chance to acquire a rare piece of American gold coinage with a documented history of survival in a safe deposit box.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Virginia family's dispute over a Smith Mountain Lake house built on a 0.7-acre lot reached an appeals court, which clarified a widow's ownership and her stepchildren's inherited shares before a partition sale
articles.summary: A family fight over who owns a lakeside house in Virginia has reached the state's Court of Appeals, where judges clarified the property rights of a widow,
articles.body: A family fight over who owns a lakeside house in Virginia has reached the state's Court of Appeals, where judges clarified the property rights of a widow, her late husband's children, and a couple who received an inherited share through a deed. The dispute focuses on a home on a 0.7-acre lot at Smith Mountain Lake in Bedford County. The Virginia Court of Appeals ruled on November 17, 2026, that Joan Cabaniss owns half of the property, while her late husband's children inherited his half through his will. One of those children later signed his share over to another couple. The decision overturned parts of an earlier ruling by the Bedford County Circuit Court and cleared the way for a partition sale. That is a court-ordered sale used to sell shared property when co-owners cannot agree on how to split it.The appeals court also clarified that Joan did not receive a life estate under her husband's will. In addition, judges said her written statement saying she planned to live in the house for the rest of her life did not change who owned the property. The ruling came in combined appeals involving Karla Cabaniss Denney v. Joan C. Cabaniss and a separate claim filed by Keith Allen Tuck and Catherine Lord Lovern-Tuck.Marriage and ownership of the lakeside homeAccording to the court's written opinion, Joan and James Cabaniss co-owned the Smith Mountain Lake property before James died in 2016. The original 1983 deed gave the property to them "jointly and equally". The appeals court decided that this wording created joint ownership without automatic transfer rights under Virginia law. That legal detail became the heart of the fight. Even though each spouse owned half of the home, James's half did not automatically go to Joan when he passed away. Instead, his share became part of his estate and followed the instructions in his will.James and Joan had a blended family. Karla Denney and Keith Cabaniss were James's children from an earlier marriage. James's will included a specific line giving Joan the right to stay in the home for as long as she wanted. It stated: "I do specifically devise unto my wife the right to live in the house for as long as she chooses." The will also spelled out what should happen if Joan decided to move out. It said: "Should my wife choose not to live in this home, I direct that it should be sold and my one-half interest in said property is to be given to my two children [Karla Denney and Keith Cabaniss]." The will also left the rest of James's estate to his two children.Widow's declaration became part of the disputeSix years after James died, Joan filed a written declaration in 2022 stating that she still lived at the home and planned to stay there for "the duration of her life". She had also transferred her interest into the Joan C. Cabaniss Trust through a deed signed in 2019. The ownership questions grew more tangled after Keith Cabaniss signed a quitclaim deed in 2020, passing his rights and interests in the property to Keith Tuck and his wife, Catherine. The deed called the transfer a gift and covered "all of his rights and interest, if any, in the property".Keith later passed away. Joan filed a partition lawsuit in 2021 to settle the ownership fight and buy out her stepchildren's shares. Because the house sat on a small 0.7-acre plot, it was hard to split the land physically among the owners. Joan therefore asked for a court-ordered sale instead of dividing the lot into separate pieces.Lower court rejected some inheritance claimsThe Bedford County Circuit Court weighed the different readings of James's will. In February 2024, it ruled that Joan was a co-owner and had the right to ask for a partition sale. The lower court also found that James's will gave her permission to live on his half of the property, along with the sole right to stay there as long as she wanted. It ruled that she had not been given a life estate.The circuit court further decided that Karla and Keith did not own direct future shares in the home. Instead, it treated their inheritance as a cash gift that would only be paid from sale money if Joan chose to move out. The lower court also dismissed the claim brought by the Tucks, ruling that Keith's quitclaim deed had passed no property rights to them. Karla and the Tucks appealed parts of that ruling, which led to the combined appeals.Appeals court clarifies who owns the propertyIn its November 17 written opinion, the Virginia Court of Appeals reviewed the original deed and the exact wording of James's will. The judges explained that the 1983 deed created shared ownership without survivorship rights. Because of that, James's half passed to his heirs when he died rather than automatically going to Joan. The court therefore confirmed that Joan kept her original half share, while James's children inherited his half under the will's catch-all clause.The judges rejected the claim that Joan had received a life estate. A life estate normally lets someone use a property for the rest of their life without giving them full ownership. The appeals court noted that Joan already owned half of the house outright on her own. It also pointed out that James's will did not include the words "for life", which Virginia law requires to create that kind of right.The judges decided that Joan's 2022 declaration had no legal power over who owned the home. Recording her plan to stay in the house could not alter the ownership rules set by the original deed and will. The court also rejected the idea that James could force Joan to sell her own half of the property simply because she eventually decided to leave. It explained that one co-owner cannot control what happens to another co-owner's share without their consent.Stepchildren inherited property, not just sale proceedsAnother major part of the ruling focused on what Karla and Keith actually inherited. The circuit court had treated their share as a legacy, which is a gift of cash or personal items from an estate. The appeals court disagreed. It found that James's will and its catch-all clause gave his children real ownership stakes in the property itself. That meant they were co-owners, not people simply waiting to collect cash after a future sale. The judges said the line asking for the house to be sold if Joan moved out could not cancel out her existing ownership rights. As a result, Karla and Keith held real ownership shares in the property right away, rather than just a future claim to sale money. This difference also changed where the Tucks stood in the case.Quitclaim deed gives Tucks standingThe appeals court overturned the lower court's finding that Keith had passed nothing to the Tucks. It ruled that Keith had inherited a real property share from his father and had properly transferred that share through the 2020 quitclaim deed. The deed alone was sufficient to hand over his rights without needing extra paperwork. As a result, Keith Tuck and Catherine Tuck became co-owners alongside Joan and Karla, giving them the legal right to take part in the partition case. The court stressed that having legal standing requires a person to show a direct financial stake in how a case turns out. Because the Tucks received Keith's property share, they met that standard.Partition sale can now proceedThe Virginia Court of Appeals answered seven specific legal questions about ownership, the meaning of James's will, the quitclaim deed, and the Tucks' right to take part in the lawsuit. It backed parts of the Bedford County Circuit Court's ruling, overturned others, and sent the case back to the lower court. The judges ordered the circuit court to move forward with the partition sale based on the appeals court's findings. The decision means Joan keeps her half of the Smith Mountain Lake house, while the other half belongs to Karla and the Tucks through the inheritance and later deed transfer. The ruling does not record a finished sale or set a final price tag. Instead, it settles the legal fight over who owns the home so the court-ordered sale can go ahead.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Texas man bought a $349,900 home and fell $4,176 behind; foreclosure warnings went to an address where mail could not be delivered, his home sold for $166,983, and an appeals court upheld $116,998 in damages
articles.summary: A Texas appeals court has upheld a $116,998 damages award to a homeowner whose property was foreclosed on without proper notice after he fell behind on
articles.body: A Texas appeals court has upheld a $116,998 damages award to a homeowner whose property was foreclosed on without proper notice after he fell behind on loan payments by just $4,176. The court ruled that the lender violated state law by sending foreclosure notices to a business address instead of the man's residential address, where he actually lived.The Texas Fourteenth Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's judgment on November 17, ruling that the foreclosure proceedings were defective because the homeowner never received proper notice of the default or the sale.Home sold for $166,983 despite being bought for $349,900The dispute involved Keith Boyer, who sold a property in Harris County, Texas, to Ryan Heasley for $349,900. The property had two separate addresses: 822 Havard, where the residential house was located, and 25523 Helms, which was used for a commercial business.After purchasing the property, Heasley fell behind on his loan payments, accumulating dues of $4,176.60.Boyer's attorney sent a notice of default and intent to accelerate the loan to the Helms address. However, the letter was returned because it could not be delivered. A second notice, informing Heasley of the loan acceleration and foreclosure sale, was also sent to the same address and returned unclaimed.Despite both notices being returned, Boyer did not send them to the Havard address, where Heasley lived and received his mail.The property subsequently went into foreclosure and was sold for $166,983, less than half the original purchase price. Heasley said he only learned about the sale after letters from the new buyers were posted on his front door.The buyers told him that he would have to leave the property or lease or purchase it back from them.Court says foreclosure notices must reach homeowner's residenceHeasley subsequently filed a wrongful foreclosure lawsuit against Boyer. A trial court awarded him $116,997.92 in damages, prompting Boyer to challenge the decision before the appeals court.Boyer argued that he had fulfilled his legal obligation by sending certified notices to the Helms address, which was listed as the property's mailing address in the deed of trust.However, the appeals court rejected the argument, pointing to the Texas Property Code's distinction between a debtor's residential property and commercial or investment property.Under Texas law, when a property being foreclosed is the debtor's residence, the notice must be sent to the person's residential address unless the debtor has formally provided a written change of address.The court noted that the Helms address was used for the commercial business and there was no evidence that anyone had lived there. Both Boyer and Heasley had identified the Havard address as the residential property.It also ruled that listing the Helms address as a mailing address in property documents did not amount to a formal written change of address for foreclosure notices.The judges stressed that foreclosure proceedings require strict compliance with legal notice requirements, particularly when a person's home is at stake.Appeals court finds inadequate notice linked to low sale priceThe court also rejected Boyer's argument that there was insufficient evidence connecting the failure to provide proper notice with the property's low foreclosure sale price.It noted that the property had been appraised at $300,000 in 2015, while Heasley had purchased it for $349,900. Yet, less than three years later, it was sold at foreclosure for around $166,983.The homeowner also testified that the foreclosure buyers later offered to sell the property back to him for $475,000. A subsequent settlement allowed him to repurchase it for $225,000.The appeals court said the evidence supported the conclusion that the defective notice had contributed to the property being sold at a significantly lower price.It ultimately rejected both grounds raised in Boyer's appeal and affirmed the trial court's judgment awarding Heasley $116,997.92.You use AI every day. articles.title: Satheesan calls it democracy as ministers confront him over unilateral decisions
articles.summary: Kerala CM V D Satheesan faces cabinet dissent over unilateral PSC and Guruvayur Devaswom appointments; says differences resolved and decisions remain collective.
articles.body: Thiruvananthapuram/New Delhi: Several ministers reportedly confronted chief minister V D Satheesan at Wednesday’s cabinet meeting, questioning his style of functioning and alleging that key decisions were being taken without adequate consultation. The development came on the day the UDF govt completed six months in office.Later, Satheesan himself acknowledged that there had been differences at the cabinet meeting but said they were resolved through discussions.“We are proud to say that there were differences of opinion in the cabinet. Everyone has the opportunity to express their views. This is democracy. This is not Pinarayi Vijayan’s cabinet,” Satheesan told a news conference in New Delhi.The unusual show of dissent exposed differences within the cabinet over collective decision-making, particularly appointments to Public Service Commission (PSC) and Guruvayur Devaswom, as well as the allocation of positions in boards and corporations.The disagreement began when Satheesan presented a list of nominees for appointment to PSC without prior discussions with other ministers. Revenue minister A P Anilkumar was reportedly the first to object, questioning how the names had been finalised without consulting other ministers or the party. The CM defended his move, saying the appointments had to be made urgently.Anilkumar also pointed out that there had been no proper consultations over the appointment of members to Guruvayur Devaswom. Power minister Sunny Joseph reportedly expressed displeasure over being kept in the dark about important decisions despite his earlier role as KPCC president. Several other ministers also reportedly joined in, alleging that the CM was taking decisions unilaterally and subsequently placing them before the cabinet for approval.According to sources, only health minister K Muraleedharan defended the CM. RSP leader and minister Shibu Baby John also raised concerns over the allocation of positions in boards and corporations, alleging that his party was not being given adequate representation.The discussion reportedly continued for nearly two-and-a-half hours, with ministers insisting that the appointments be reconsidered. The differences were eventually resolved through discussions, with the demands of various factions taken into account and a few nominees changed.The disagreement was particularly evident over Guruvayur Devaswom appointments. Ministers A P Anilkumar, M Liju, Bindu Krishna and O J Janeesh had reportedly initially refused to sign the file, alleging that the nominees had been finalised without consulting them. Only Muraleedharan and K A Thulasi had signed it initially.In New Delhi, the CM said the UDF was not a group of sycophants and that ministers were free to disagree with him. Even the youngest minister, Janeesh, could look him in the eye and express a contrary opinion, he said.“Team UDF remains Team UDF. All decisions taken by the UDF cabinet are collective decisions. If we cannot reach a consensus on an issue, we will defer it,” Satheesan said. However, he declined to comment directly on whether the PSC appointments had triggered the differences, saying all the proposed names were appropriate.The CM also criticised the previous LDF govt’s handling of the PM SHRI agreement, alleging that it was signed without proper cabinet discussions.Highlighting his govt’s achievements in six months, he said 568 projects had been completed in the first 100 days. He expressed confidence that the govt would deliver further results over the next six months and reiterated its commitment to compassionate and people-oriented governance.The CM also met PM Narendra Modi in the capital. “We discussed key issues concerning Keralam’s development and sought the Union govt’s continued support for the state’s progress and welfare,” the CM posted on ‘X’.Meanwhile, responding to reporters’ queries on the issue, home minister Ramesh Chennithala said: “Unlike the Marxist party, where opinions are imposed, we discuss problems to resolve them. The decisions are taken unitedly by us. There is no difference of opinion in the cabinet, party or UDF.”Stay updated with the latest Thiruvananthapuram news. Download the TOI App.
